definition: The rules extraction system (RULES) family is a family of inductive learning that includes several covering algorithms.
details: This family is used to build a predictive model based on given observation. It works based on the concept of separate-and-conquer to directly induce rules from a given training set and build its knowledge repository. Algorithms under RULES family are usually available in data mining tools, such as KEEL and WEKA, known for knowledge extraction and decision making.

explainer.lead: A family of inductive learning algorithms that build predictive models by inducing rules directly from training data. It matters because it produces an interpretable knowledge repository rather than an opaque model.

tiers.eli5: Instead of memorising the whole book, you jot down a short list of rules that explain most of it.
tiers.practitioner: Used to induce classification rules from a training set via separate-and-conquer; a common pitfall is that greedy rule covering can overfit noisy data unless rules are pruned or limited.
tiers.paperLevel: Inductive learning family using the separate-and-conquer strategy: rules are induced one at a time, each covering part of the training set, with covered examples removed before the next rule. Limits: rule sets can grow large and greedy induction gives no global optimality guarantee.

explainer.example: On a training set of labelled observations, a RULES-family algorithm induces a set of if-then rules that together cover the examples and serve as the predictive model.
